race.name: Chasing Cancellara Zürich to Andermatt
race.tagline: A 203.5-kilometer Alpine road ultra from Zürich over Klausen Pass to Andermatt.

vitals.prize_purse: Published rankings; no cash purse published

climate.description: A pre-dawn start, exposed passes, and more than fifteen hours of possible weather create cold, rain, wind, and rapid temperature-change risk.

terrain.surface: Paved public roads from Zürich through Glarnerland, over Klausen Pass, and into Andermatt.

fondo_rating.scoring_notes: Grade uses the organizer's completed 2026 roadbook: 203.5 km, 4,335 m, four named climbing sectors, 2:00 AM start, five aid stations, timing, moto and medical support, neutral service, luggage transfer, and 5:00 PM finish cutoff. Formula: 52/70 = 74. Re-grade when the next edition is announced. Sources: https://www.chasingcancellara.com/zurich-andermatt and the official 2026 roadbook.

distance.explanation: The official 2026 roadbook measured 203.5 km, just beyond the 200 km ultra threshold.[2][3]

climbing.explanation: The roadbook publishes 4,335 m of ascent, beyond the 4,000 m mountain threshold.[3]

descent_technicality.explanation: Klausen Pass and the high-Alpine approach to Andermatt demand sustained switchback descending.[2][3]

road_surface.explanation: The event uses paved Swiss public roads without a cobbled showcase.[2][3]

climate_risk.explanation: A 2:00 AM start and multiple Alpine passes create real cold, storm, and temperature-swing exposure.[2][3]

altitude.explanation: Klausen Pass and the Andermatt finish sit in the 1,000-2,000 m rubric band.[3]

logistics.explanation: Zürich is a major transport hub, while the Andermatt finish requires point-to-point planning.[2]

prestige.explanation: Fabian Cancellara's name and the Alpine route attract international recognition without iconic mass-event scale.[1][2]

organization.explanation: Timing, moto escort, ambulance, neutral service, route signage, luggage transfer, and five aid stations support the grade.[2][3]

scenic_experience.explanation: Lake Zürich, Glarnerland, Klausen Pass, and an Andermatt finish form a genuine high-Alpine showcase.[2][3]

community_culture.explanation: Series identity, rankings, a finisher meal, and multiple team formats create a solid event culture.[1][2]

field_depth.explanation: Timed solo and team categories with official rankings create structured competition.[2][3]

value.explanation: The 2026 package was comprehensive, but Swiss pricing and no next-edition fee keep value neutral.[2]

expenses.explanation: Swiss lodging, a point-to-point trip, and premium entry make this a destination-level expense.[2]

course_description.character: The 2026 course left Zürich at 2:00 AM, crossed rolling terrain by Lake Zürich, climbed through Glarnerland and Klausen Pass, then finished after the final ascent to Andermatt. Drafting was prohibited after kilometer 30.4 outside specified team categories.
course_description.signature_challenge: Climbing Klausen Pass and then another 20.7-kilometer, 915-meter ascent toward Andermatt after more than 180 kilometers.

logistics.lodging_strategy: Sleep in Zürich before the 2:00 AM start and book post-race lodging in Andermatt.
logistics.transport: Use organizer luggage transfer and Swiss rail for the point-to-point return.
logistics.food: Five aid stations plus a finisher meal were included in 2026.

history.origin_story: Chasing Cancellara evolved from Fabian Cancellara's original chase format into distinct Swiss road races, including this point-to-point Alpine ultra.
notable_moments: 2026: 203.5 km / 4,335 m course over Klausen Pass to Andermatt
history.reputation: The series' complete high-Alpine endurance test: long enough to be an ultra and steep enough to punish ordinary fondo pacing.

biased_opinion.verdict: The Best Complete Race in the Series
biased_opinion.summary: Zürich-Andermatt has the cleanest sporting argument of the three races: more than 200 kilometers, more than 4,000 meters, a 2:00 AM start, Klausen Pass, and a final climb after the legs are already empty.
biased_opinion.bottom_line: A serious Alpine road ultra with excellent support, but no dated TrainingPeaks product should open until the next organizer roadbook lands.

final_verdict.one_liner: Two hundred kilometers, 4,335 meters, Klausen Pass, and a final climb to Andermatt.
final_verdict.should_you_race: Yes if a 2:00 AM Alpine ultra sounds like a goal rather than a warning. Wait for the next official edition before fixing your training calendar.
final_verdict.alternatives: Bern-Zermatt is longer; Granfondo Vaduz keeps the timed climbing without the all-day ultra.
